Having been a junior officer, I am wondering who will perform the duties of orderly officers. Of the 3,000 officers the minister mentioned only 532 lieutenants and second-lieutenants. The balance is not there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is only one orderly officer for each establishment, and we have not that many establishments.

I was referring to
orderly officers for units. How many lieutenants are we to have? Then, I asked a question wrhich I believe was overlooked, with respect to civil servants in the army. We are to have an army with a personnel of 25,000. If there are 11,000 to 12,000 civil servants, does that mean that we are to have
25,000	plus the civil servants or 25,000 inclusive of the civil servants?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It will be 25,000 plus
the civil servants. I can assure my hon. friend that the number of civil servants in the Department of National Defence will be considerably decreased. The number has been decreased since last year, and as demobilization is completed it will be decreased still further. My hon. friend must understand that in the period between demobilizing the old force and setting up the new interim force it is necessary to employ civil servants. A number of temporary employees have been taken on to handle war service gratuities, dependents allowances and other services. It is expected that these services will be closed out in a short time, which will permit of an extensive decrease in the civil staff of the department. The number of civil servants employed includes considerable casual labour which it is necessary to employ during the period of demobilization.
We are to have a uniformed force of 25,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is right.

Of that number, 7,052 are to be in the brigade group, which leaves about 18,000 odd for other regimental duties such as national defence headquarters, the commands, the districts, the training staff, and what have you. How many officers will there be at national defence headquarters? What is to be the establishment of the commands? What is to be the establishment of the districts? How many personnel will be distributed among militia or reserve units for training purposes? It looks as though out of a total force of 25,000 we shall have only 7,500 men actually available in case of emergency. Por instance, there are 3,049 officers; are there to be, 3,049 batmen? Will those men be taken out of the training establishment? Batmen do not do general duties, as the parliamentary assistant knows.
They should.

That is right, they
should, but they do not. I can take you around Ottawa here and show you some of those men cutting lawns. How many staff

Supply-Defence-Army
cars are to be run? The other day I saw six staff cars and a station wagon lined up on Bay street in Toronto. How are you going to have any men in the army if you permit this sort of thing to go on?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend
has considerable knowledge of military establishments. If he wants me to give him the details of every unit of our peacetime establishment, including the duties of every one, and what there will be in the way of transport, in the way of armament and so on, I shall be glad to do it. I have not that information at hand, but I can give it to my hon. friend in detail, and I think it will keep him busy during the recess.

I want to make sure
we are getting value for the money we are putting up. Everyone knows thaft we must have an efficient service. I bring up these matters to point out the stupid expenditures that are being made at this time.

People are beginning to wonder at the ramifications of the Department of National Defence. I have a letter from the Minister of National Defence stating that his department intends to publish more copies of the famous French-English military dictionary. It may be possible that some of these staff cars and station wagons are being used by the publishing and printing staffs of the Department of National Defence. I am sure that members of this house and of the senate were pleased to receive copies of that seven pound book, which can be utilized for practically no purpose whatsoever. According to the Minister of National Defence, $25,000 has been spent by the department to publish 1,100 copies, or approximately $25- per book. As I say, the minister has stated that the department intends to put out additional copies to be sold by the department. Twenty-five thousand dollars may seem a small amount compared with other government expenditures, but we are told that additional money is to be spent in publishing this book and in making salesmen out of members of the staff of the Department of National Defence. I do not think the government needs to rely upon the sale of French-English dictionaries in order to provide revenue with which to run the Department of National Defence. I should like the parliamentary assistant fo state whether it is intended to print additional copies for the purpose of sale, not only in Canada out abroad.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I wish to assure my hon. friend that none of the staff cars he may see circulating around Ottawa are used by the
publishers of the department. The book to which he refers was printed by the king's printer, and I have no knowledge of additional copies having been ordered.
Has not the demand been brisk ?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know, because that is also handled by the king's printer. I have not kept a chart of the sales of that particular item, and I do not know whether the demand is brisk. I can assure my hon. friend that at times I have found that book very useful, and I am sure other people have found it useful.
. Mr. FERGUSON: I should be very glad if the department would get out a dictionary which would help members of this house to learn French, perhaps at a cost of $3 or $4. but I do not think it is humanly possible to learn to speak the French language or the English language from this book which has been published at a cost of $25. In my opinion that is simply squandering the taxpayers' money. I hope the parliamentary assistant speaks with authority when he says that no more of these books will be published, or that no more time of people on the payroll of the Department of National Defence will be taken up in connection with the publishing and sale of this book. However, the fact remains that the Minister of National Defence did state to me that he intended to print more of these books for sale.
The other night several questions were asked with respect to the personnel of the signal corps at Yellowknife, Dawson and Whitehorse, and these have not been answered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked how many signal corps personnel were stationed at Whitehorse, Yellowknife and Dawson City. The figures are as follows: Whitehorse, 1 officer, 7 other ranks; Yellowknife, 12 other ranks; Dawson City, 4 other ranks. My hon. friend asked whether they get annual leave. It has not been the policy to grant leave to personnel on these stations, because in the summer they cannot be spared and in the winter transportation is difficult. This is made plain to them when they volunteer for this service, and they receive extra pay on that account. Their leave is cumulative and they can take it after they have served two years. Compassionate leave is also granted, and transportation paid in such cases. To summarize, the condition is that they serve two years, they receive extra pay for this type of service and their leave is cumulative.
Supply-Defence-Army
The air force for many months have had a plane running between Edmonton and Whitehorse. Perhaps some' arrangements could be made with the air force to bring these men out on leave.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be glad to investigate the possibilities.

I desire to raise a question which has been brought to my attention by a number of ex-servicemen of this war, many of whom have served in both great wars. It is the vexed question of the clothing allowance granted on discharge. As the minister knows, from September 1, 1939, until October 31, 1943, the clothing allowance for those who were discharged from His Majesty's Canadian armed forces was $35. According to a return which the government brought down in a response to a question I asked in the house on June 10 no less than 96,561 members of the Canadian armed forces received on discharge a clothing allowance of only $35. That is pretty nearly
100,000	of our Canadian soldiers, which is no small number. Then the government, yielding to public and parliamentary and largely, shall I say, opposition pressure, increased the clothing allowance to $65 per person. That remained in effect, according to the return, from November 1, 1943, to July 31, 1944, and there were discharges during that period to the number of 42,559. At the expiry of that period on July 31, 1944, the government, again yelding to persistent pressure, brought the clothing allowance up to $100 per person. In the meantime a total of 140,000 of our men who had enlisted and been discharged, and many of whom had seen service in both wars, found that while everybody discharged after July 31, 1944, got $100 clothing allowance, they had received many of them, only $35 and the others $65 clothing allowance. That seems to be rank discrimination no matter which way you look at it, because there was no substantial difference between the cost of outfitting a man discharged from the armed forces in any of those periods, and if it was right to give a man a clothing allowance of SlOO after August 1, 1944, it was obviously right that every man discharged from the beginning of the war until August 1, 1944, should have received the same amount.
I am going to appeal to the parliamentary assistant to-day to be a little more considerate than the minister himself appeared to be when I brought this matter up before, because many members of our armed forces, to the numbers I have mentioned are rankling under what they feel is an injustice done to them in the clothing allowance granted. I

ask the parliamentary assistant to review this whole matter again and to see to it that these men are given their just deserts with respect to the clothing allowance.	.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be pleased to have the matter looked into again.

The breakdown of officers of the permanent force which the parliamentary assistant gave a little while ago shows 100 officers of the rank of full colonel or above. That number in my opinion is extravagantly large. I can think of only from thirty to thirty-five jobs in the army in Canada which require an officer of the rank of full colonel or above. There are some eleven military districts and five commands, making a total of sixteen. There is one brigade group, bringing the total to seventeen. If you allow fifteen at N.D.H.Q., which is a very liberal allowance of officers to serve as heads of services, chiefs of staffs and their chief assistants, you have thirty-two altogether. Add another one for the Yukon, now that we are looking after the Alaska highway, and that brings the total to thirty-three. In any event thirty-five is the absolute maximum of jobs that I can think of requiring an officer of the rank of full colonel or above. I should like very much to know what the government are going to do with the other sixty-five. It looks to me as though they had been pushed into very soft jobs, carrying a rank which the job itself does not justify and did not justify even under active service conditions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have given my hon. friend the proposed establishment. As to whether we have too many high-ranking officers or whether they are occupying posts where they are just filling soft jobs, as my hon. friend stated, in the army, as in any department of government or in any private concern, you must have men at the top to run the job efficiently, and you pay them according to what they are worth and according to the work they do. That is what we intend to do in the army. My hon. friend will recall that under the new set-up of pay there is no longer in the army what we used to call the classified staff pay, under which system officers serving at headquarters receive in addition to the pay of their rank special pay for staff work. That has been done away with, and I think rightly, if I may express my humble opinion. But it makes for this situation, that an officer in order to get the pay which is adequate for the service he renders must be given the rank which calls for that pay. I hope my hon. friend will believe that this policy is justifiable.

Supply-Defence-Army
I am afraid I am not satisfied with that answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I did not expect it.

As I say, under the army system we have in this country, which is modeled on the British system and corresponds fairly well with the United States system, certain jobs carry certain ranks; and as far as our army here in Canada is concerned, I have yet to be shown why we should have more than thirty-four jobs which would carry the rank of full colonel. In my opinion we just have not the jobs. The army is not big enough in peacetime to have that number. I think we are just top-heavy with ranking officers. If I said that it was a matter of creating "soft jobs" for them, I am sorry. I did not mean that they were soft jobs; I meant that these officers were given jobs with inflated rank and, therefore, an inflated rate of pay. The jobs may be much bigger than some which officers with a rank or two higher are performing.

May I direct the
attention of the committee for a short time to the Alaska highway, which, all hon. members will recall was constructed by the United States through northwestern Canada while the war was on. It will be remembered that there was particularly constructed a stretch of highway about fifteen hundred miles in length extending from Fort St. John to Fairbanks, Alaska, at an expense which has been estimated at between S98 million and $133 million. An all weather road and an all year route, it is graded twenty-four feet wide and capable of cariying a tremendous volume of traffic. The estimated cost of maintenance of this road is between $3 million and $5 million, according to the Great Falls Tribune, in an article published on October 7, 1945. This road, as hon. members know, has been turned over to the Dominion of Canada. It is of exceedingly great importance to us, we will say, in connection with business and tourist traffic, and we will discuss it from that point of view. I should like to know what the government is doing concerning this road. I understand that it is under the care of the Department of National Defence.
Supply-Defence-Army

There are several aspects of this matter which, I believe, should be looked into by the committee at this time. The first has to do with the maintenance of the road. We can either let the road stand idle and deteriorate, as it would naturally do, or keep it in a state of good repair. It is extremely important for the committee to know what the government is doing in this regard; how much has been spent since V-J day; in what respect it has been spent; with what results, and who is doing the work. I think we as a committee should look into that. Perhaps someone who is doing the work is getting more pay thafi he ought to get, or maybe is getting too little.
Another matter: is the road open for tourist traffic? Hon. members know how important the tourist trade is to Canada. They have been informed, as a result of the activities of the hon. member for Davenport, of the almost fairyland attractions of that northern area. They will, therefore, realize that there are great tourist possibilities in that country if this great highway is opened for tourist traffic. I should like the minister to tell us something about that.
Then I think it would be a good thing for us to know to what extent the highway is available for commercial traffic. If heavy trucks are being allowed to carry oil and other heavy loads over the highway, it may be that the highway has deteriorated. We ought to know something about the government's policy in that respect.
Obviously, if this road is to be of the greatest value to the Dominion of Canada tributary roads should be built into it from the various provinces. It is quite conceivable that there should be one, say, from Winnipeg, one from Saskatoon, and one coming in from British Columbia. The obvious thing, I would think, for the federal government to do would be to invite the cooperation of the four western provinces that are contiguous to the road in building suitable highways which could be used in cases of emergency for almost any kind of traffic which it may be found necessary to carry over them. I should like to know to what extent the government has considered that matter and how great its progress has been in this regard.
Another matter which should be looked into is the development of the resources along the Alaska highway. There is a wide variety of resources. We have timber, minerals, areas of good land which could be used for agricultural purposes, and so on, and a good deal of fishing is possible there. It seems to me that a wise policy organized in conjunction with the provinces could bring about a condition
[Mr. Blackmnrp.l
under which it would be much less expensive for the dominion to maintain this highway at that standard of quality at which I think the United States would be justified in expecting us to maintain it, and at which our own national safety would dictate that we should maintain it.
Obviously, if there is to be any considerable use of the road, either for commercial purposes or for tourist purposes, there should be such facilities as service stations along the way and even restaurants and other necessary conveniences. I think it would be interesting for the minister to tell us something about what is being done in that regard, whether the government has a policy of encouraging those who might wish to establish such facilities along the road and what succes it is having in that regard.
There is a section of the road which has not yet been completed. It is the section between Edmonton, and Dawson Creek. There is about a 200-mile stretch of road there which has not yet been completed so that it could be used in an effective way in case of emergency or for ordinary commercial purposes. For obvious reasons, this section should be built at as early a day as possible. Would the minister tell the committee what the plan of the government is with regard to this matter and what has already been done? I wish to ask a number of questions, and so that the minister may have an opportunity to reply to them in an orderly way I will read them and then send the list over to him.
1.	Is the Alaska highway being maintained? How much money has been expended since V-J day? In what sorts of maintenance was the money expended, and who did the work-government companies or agencies or private companies and agencies?
2.	Is tourist traffic being permitted by the government? If not, why not?
3.	Is the highway available for ordinary commercial traffic?
4.	Have any steps been taken to obtain cooperation of the four western provinces in constructing high-class highways connecting with the highway to enhance its value?
5.	Has anything been done to stimulate the development of resources contiguous to the highway?
6.	What has been or is being done to encourage the establishment and development of facilities for services for traffic along the Alaska highway?
7.	What measures has the government adopted or planned to complete the stretch from Edmonton to D lwson Creek, about 200 miles?

Supply-Defence-Army
Perhaps the minister will allow me to say a few words first, and he can reply to me at the same time. I may be able to help him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: You probably can.

Having been over much of the Alaska highway, I know something about it. The hon. member for Lethbridge has said something about it, and I will begin with the last question he asked in regard to the roadway from Edmonton to Dawson Creek. I would advise that this road be projected straight north west in as direct a route as possible to Grande Prairie.
Through Whitecourt.

Yes, through Whitecourt to Grande Prairie, then following the present roadway to Dawson Creek, where you connect up with the Alaska highway which now starts at Dawson Creek. The original programme was to start it at Fort St. John. From Dawson Creek north it is a good roadway but it will require considerable attention. In reply to a question asked earlier in the session, a minister -I forget who it was-said that the government contemplated that it would cost about 85,000,000 a year to keep the roadway in proper operation, and I for one would be well pleased if they could keep it in adequate condition for operation at a cost of four or five million dollars a year. It is found in the spring that in a number of cases the bridges are taken out, because of the mountainous rivers rising as high as forty feet in a night as a result of the rapid melting of snows in the mountains which the road runs through for a considerable distance, or from heavy rains. That, however, is not an insurmountable obstacle. Besides, the maintenance of the roadway and repairs to bridges would give the department a splendid opportunity to train their engineers. I suggest that the government has a highly desirable school there for its engineering department in the maintenance of the Alaska highway, and the money will not be misspent, because, after all, the engineers must be trained and this work affords a practical opportunity for training them. Moreover, the government will have to maintain quite a staff of all sorts of men to assist the engineers, and they will have to give them practical training for the purpose. The Alaska highway would offer a golden opportunity for the practical training of all such men as are associated with the engineers in the construction of military works of any description.
The hon. member spoke of other roadways. I suggest that the defence department be employed to connect up the roadway that now
runs west from Peace River through Grim-shaw, but which does not, though it should, connect with Fort St. John. There again the department would have an excellent opportunity for training its men. Of course, it would have to cooperate with the British Columbia and Alberta governments but I understand that those governments are willing to cooperate and are themselves interested in promoting the construction of the roadway. Cooperation would also be necessary with the Saskatchewan government, which desires very greatly that the latter roadway should be completed. I agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge that the Alaska highway would be a remarkable tourist route, particularly the north end of it, because I doubt whether there is any place in America where one can enjoy such grandeur. There is no more magnificent scenery, no more striking landscape than is to be seen from Fort Nelson north, particularly as you get up to and beyond Watson lake. In that area Canada has a perfect paradise of tourist attraction.
As far as minerals are concerned, near Watson lake they are projecting a number of gold mines which will be profitable. I do not wish to take up any .more time, but I strongly endorse the suggestion that the department use such men as are required to keep that road in first-class shape, thereby providing a roadway to a tourist paradise and at the same time furnishing actual practical work for the training of engineers and all others associated with them. I suggest that it would return a rich harvest.

I am greatly interested in this question, and I regret very much to take up a few minutes of your time, Mr. Chairman, of which I have been very sparing; but if this government is to spend more money on the Alaska highway, I suggest to you, sir, that it should be done in the way it has been done throughout the war, from Edmonton to the town of Athabaska northwesterly, crossing Slave river, south of Slave lake and along the shores of that beautiful lake to Peace river. That road carried immense traffic throughout the war when the highway was constructed from Dawson Creek to Whitehorse and beyond and hundreds and thousands of trucks traveled from Edmonton, damaging the road to a considerable extent in consequence. That was the result of extensive and heavy traffic. If the dominion government is to enter into an expenditure this side of Dawson Creek, undoubtedly it should be from Edmonton to Athabaska and from Athabaska to Smith, and on to the Peace river south of Lesser Slave lake. A bridge was constructed over the river west of Slave
Supply-Defence-Army

lake, costing a large sum of money, in order to serve the Alaska highway. It is the proper place to spend more money; and I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that if the Department of National Defence decides to enter upon this undertaking and take over the road from Dawson Creek to Edmonton, if they undertake further expenditure within the province of Alberta it should be on the road to the town of Athabaska and northwesterly from there to the Peace river country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for Davenport and the last speaker for giving me all this information on the local situation in connection with the Alaska highway. I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge. I know the importance of the highway in that section of the country, not only in regard to tourist trade but also in regard to future development of the natural resources of that great region; and, as he mentioned, from the point of view of defence. The hon. member asked a series of questions, which I shall answer as far as may be possible.
His first question was, is the Alaska highway being maintained and how much money has been expended since V-J day; and on what maintenance work has the money been expended? The northwest highway system, as my hon. friend knows, was taken over by the Canadian government, by the Department of National Defence, on April 1 last. Prior to that, the work had been done and the expenditure made by the United States. In connection with taking over the road a unit of Canadian engineers was sent there in January, 1946. The actual expenditure by the Canadian government up to the time the highway was taken over was $188,344. Since we have taken over the highway, to July 31 we have spent $625,000 in operation and maintenance, and the personnel we have there number 245 service personnel and 416 civilians. Of the civilians, the great majority were already engaged in the maintenance of the highway, and were taken over by us. I want to assure the hon. member for Lethbridge and also the hon. member for Davenport that, in taking over this highway, the department has contemplated its use as a future training ground for our engineers in the post-war army, and undoubtedly it will be used for that purpose. All the work on the highway is being done by the personnel I have just mentioned, under the direction of the commander of the northwest highway system.
With regard to tourist traffic, I am told that at present tourists may go on the highway but must first obtain a permit from

the acting special commissioner for the Canadian government in Edmonton. They must show that they are in good health and that their vehicles are in serviceable condition for the trip up the highway and back. My hon. friend will understand that this is necessary at the present time in view of the lack of facilities along the highway, and it was only prudent on the part of the authorities to follow this course. The highway is also available for commercial traffic, again subject to the approval of the special commissioner. I am informed-and this information is not official but comes to me like the information I have received from the hon. member for Davenport-that in July some 897 vehicles, both passenger cars and trucks, made the trip over the highway.
As to the possible extension of the highway to join with other highways in the various provinces, I am informed that at present this question is under consideration with the governments of Alberta and British Columbia.
I believe my hon. friend also asked what was being done in connection with the development of the natural resources of that region. As he knows, that matter comes under the Department of Mines and Resources, and I am afraid I would not be in a position to give him that information.
The question of the completion of the stretch between. Edmonton and Dawson Creek is, I realize, an important matter. I did not realize it before, but I understand now that it is a controversial question. I am afraid I am not in a position to give the hon. member any information. It would appear that this might be a matter under the control of the government of Alberta, since it is a question of highway construction. However, I am sure the matter will be given study in connection with the future use of the highway and the development of the region.

I appreciate the information the parliamentary assistant has given in his answers to the questions asked by the hon. member for Lethbridge. I should like to make one or two further observations and ask one or two questions. Has anything been done as yet by the department to connect the Great Slave lake area by a cross-road to the Alaska highway, and also the Great Bear lake basin, where they have discovered many important minerals? I ask these questions because it seems to me if the Alaska highway is properly to serve Canada in times of stress as well as in times of peace, feeder roads will have to be built linking these great mineral areas with the strategic highways along which the traffic of the northwest runs. As the hon. gentleman

Supply-Defence-Army
knows, the provincial government of Alberta, in collaboration and cooperation with the dominion government, at the present time is [DOT] building the Grimshaw-Slave Lake highway. That is a thrust of about 200 miles straight north of Grimshaw, which is just west of Peace River town. That is to get into the Mackenzie basin. Down the Mackenzie basin is an easy grade, which has been surveyed several times. I believe the province of Alberta originally recommended that this be the route of the Alaska highway, but that recommendation was not followed. I further believe that since then it has been decided it was a mistake not to follow that recommendation. However, the road is there and I believe it can serve a very useful purpose. -In the Slave lake area, as well as in the Great Bear lake area and the Norman Wells area, we have already developed huge mineral resources. WTe also have the Canol pipeline, which runs across from the Norman Wells area into Alaska. Some kind of tractor road, or perhaps just a primitive trail, was built across there, and I was wondering if the department intends to develop that into a permanent road, so that in due course the pipeline may be able to serve the needs of the great northwest, whenever the oil from Norman Wells is needed. If the parliamentary assistant would answer those questions, then I should like to say one word with respect to a matter which has caused a little difference of opinion here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to give any specific answer about the particular routes, roads or highways the hon. member mentioned. All I can tell him is that the whole development of that region and the further roads to extend from the Alaska highway is at present under study. I am afraid I cannot give anything further.

As the department develops its plans, there is one thing which could be kept in mind, with profit, and I offer it only as a suggestion. It might be considered when the plans are being laid for the development of the northern country, and the highway itself. It is quite conceivable that that great northwestern highway might become of tremendous value to Canada in a time of stress. Its value would depend upon whether it is linked with the great industrial parts of America, along which route from such industrial areas materials might be moved quickly for defence purposes.
For a number of years the province of Alberta, the state of Montana, and other areas in northwestern United States and in Canada have organized bodies to study this highway, and the need for it. They have advocated the most direct possible route from
Great Falls in Montana to Lethbridge, Calgary and Edmonton, and up to Dawson Creek and Fort St. John.
As to the route, the province of Alberta, in constructing the link between the international boundary line and Lethbridge just last year, kept in mind the possible need of a military highway. They have built in that link of about seventy-five miles the finest example of what could be a military highway, that I have seen in Canada. I understand that it is ready for hard-surfacing this year. They have also been improving the route between Lethbridge and Edmonton. Two or three years ago the province of Alberta completed a survey between Edmonton and Grande Prairie by way of Whitecourt, a northwest route which obviates the necessity of going clear around through Athabaska and along the shores of Slave lake. It cuts off approximately 100 miles in the distance between Dawson Creek and Edmonton, runs through a country where the grades would probably be easy, and where the country could easily be developed.
That survey is complete, and the information is available. Some day we shall see the necessity of having the most direct route for military purposes. The parliamentary assistant has stated that the development of other highways through centres now served will have to be left to the province. I say the province is fully aware of its responsibility in that respect and is to-day improving the road by way of Athabaska and up through the southern Peace river.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be pleased to draw the minister's attention to what the hon. member has said.

I can add a word for the minister's benefit with respect to the first route mentioned by the hon. member for Peace River, namely the route from Norman Wells extending 650 miles across two ranges of mountains to Whitehorse. That is another area where departmental engineers and those associated with them will have plenty of opportunity to develop themselves. I have been over the east end of that route from Norman Wells to stop 41, a distance of something less than 100 miles, and I was over the west end of the route for about 100 miles. At the time I was there the roadway was open all the way through, but when one comes to the two ranges of mountains through which the roadway runs a tractor would be required to pull a car up the grade. I do not believe it was ever completed to the extent that anyone leaving Whitehorse could ride through in his motor car to Norman Wells without the assistance of a tractor to get up the grades. Further
Supply-Dejence-Army

than that, one could go through only in a motor car with high wheels, one of the old fashioned type, because of the mountain creeks.
This is an area in which the department will have one of the best opportunities possible to train engineers and all personnel who will assist the army engineers. Since the government must maintain an engineering staff and train it, I would say this is a fine place to do it. If they ever do, through their engineering service, make the Whitehorse-Norman Wells route passable for cars, it will make available a tourist route the like of which few human eyes have seen. It almost beggars description, so far as I have seen it. It is a marvellous area, and I have no doubt that if it is once completed it will be so great an attraction for tourist traffic it will pay for itself.

The parliamentary
assistant will have noticed that a large percentage of the Alaska highway, as it will be in its completed form, will be built through Alberta. This necessitates tremendous expenditures.
Up to parallel 60.

This runs through a relatively sparsely settled area in Alberta. While we are discussing this matter, I would suggest that the parliamentary assistant should urge upon the minister to take under serious consideration the advisability of setting aside a government appropriation for Alberta, to assist the province in the building of this highway. There is no suggestion that the province would not ultimately build it, but perhaps, owing to scarcity of money, it might not be able to build it soon enough. Would the parliamentary assistant bring this matter to the attention of the minister?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be pleased to do so.
I asked the minister for particulars about the purchase of property. He said he would get them. If the item is passed now, when shall I get those particulars.

This morning the hon. member for Lake Centre asked the minister to produce a letter from the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police dealing with certain alleged wrongdoing in connection with the use of army rejection certificates. The minister said he would give the request consideration. He is not here this afternoon, and I should like to know when we shall get this information, if the item passes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The minister did say he was asking that the matter be looked into, in the files. He also said it might be necessary to refer to the district, if correspondence had taken place between the district and the mounted police. If there is any correspondence to table I shall gladly table it at the same time as I table any other information, when the air services are before the committee.

I have a question in connection with properties taken over by the department from private owners, which have now been turned back to War Assets Corporation, and which are now being resold by War Assets Corporation to the former owners. Many of these properties were used for training purposes in connection with bombing, %nd so on. I believe there were two or three around Sussex with which the parliamentary assistant will be familiar. They have been turned over to War Assets Corporation, and private citizens have made arrangements to buy them. But these arrangements have been held up for months, the difficulty being that the properties have to be decontaminated- I believe that is the term used. Are steps being taken to decontaminate the properties which have been turned over to War Assets? If not, can this work be speeded up, because I know a lot of men who want to get back on these properties are being held up?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The minute a property
is declared surplus and it goes into the hands of War Assets our responsibility ceases, so to speak. The process followed by War Assets has absolutely nothing to do with us. In cases where a property was taken over, say, from a municipality, for use as a training ground without any buildings being erected, the property is remitted to the municipality without having to go through WTar Assets. But if there has been any construction it must go through War Assets.

The properties I have referred to are near Essex and they are made up of a number of farms which were taken over. These properties should be decontaminated before being handed over to War Assets, and I understand the difficulty is to get the Department of National Defence to do this work. The arrangements made by War Assets to sell these properties are held up because they are not decontaminated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will look into the matter right away.

I should like to say a
word about the supplying of equipment to the reserve army, particularly to those units using technical equipment. The minister

Labour Conditions
made a statement in connection with the supply of equipment to the reserve army of Canada, but, so far as I know, armoured regiments and SP artillery regiments in particular have received only small amounts of equipment in the way of tanks and SP guns. I am particularly familiar with an anti-tank regiment composed of four batteries. Each battery is supposed to have twelve guns, but so far they have been supplied only with two SP guns which, in my opinion, is not sufficient for training purposes.
I would request the department to be as generous as possible in the matter of supplying equipment to reserve units. They have a difficult time in attracting recruits and carrying on training under the best of circumstances. With the large amount of equipment left on our hands at the end of the war, I should think it would be readily possible to supply these reserve units with what they need in the way of tanks, SP guns, transport vehicles, signal equipment, signal vehicles and so on. I cannot emphasize too strongly the necessity of the department being generous to the reserve units in the matter of supplying equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF WAGE AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
A report has just been received by telephone from Mr. F. W. Edge, director of labour relations, Canadian National Railways, that his negotiations with the presidents, vice presidents and general chairmen of the various labour organizations representing all the employees of the Canadian National Railways, the Ontario Northern Railway and all the subsidiaries of the Canadian National
Railways, representing in all approximately
115,000	men, have been successful. At one o'clock to-day the president and executive vice-president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. R. C. Vaughan and Mr. N. B. Walton, approved an agreement which had been entered into by Mr. Edge with the heads of the various organizations, calling for an increase in the case of maintenance of way men of eight cents per hour, and of all other organizations of ten cents per hour, effective June 1, 1946, and deferring consideration with respect to conditions until February 1, 1947. The only organization in connection with which the negotiations have not been concluded is the brotherhood of railway trainmen. These negotiations are being conducted separately, and it is expected that an agreement will be consummated in the near future.
The reason the maintenance of way men were offered and have agreed to a rate lower than other occupations is that they had a two cent adjustment in their wage rates in April, 1946. It is of interest to note that a number of the men are affiliated with the Canadian congress of labour, and the negotiations have been conducted on their behalf by Mr. A. R. Mosher, president of the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees and other transport workers. An application is being made by Mr. Edge on behalf of both the employees and the company to the national war labour board for approval.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National
Revenue) moved the second reading of bill No. 391, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, while this bill is short and may appear to some to be innocuous, I hope that in the discussion we shall realize the great importance of this measure. This bill contemplates the extension of the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and it should be considered carefully before being
Radio Broadcasting

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
adopted, especially since that expansion, in part at least, is to be at the expense of certain private stations. The bill raises the whole question of the relationship between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private stations. It places at the disposal of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a blank cheque with which to carry on this great programme of expansion.
The bill embodies some of the recommendations contained in the report of the special committee on radio broadcasting which was tabled a few days ago. Three of the four sections of the bill deal with recommendations from that report. At the outset I should like to emphasize that the report was not unanimous. It represents the recommendations of the Liberal-C.C.F. majority on the committee, but it was opposed by the Progressive Conservative and Social Credit members.
The report recommends lavish commitments and carries a complete approval of everything the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has ever done or proposes to do. In the second place, it proposes to be more than lavish in meeting all the requests of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In the third place, it proposes, as the bill itself indicates, to be lavish with the money of the people of Canada in giving support to its programme.
Good work was done in the committee. A number of facts of the highest importance were brought before the public. The work of the committee was not done exhaustively, because there are certain things that should have been done and should have been treated in the report which were to some extent side-stepped both in the report and in the bill. Matters are also dealt with in the report which were not before the committee when it was taking evidence.
I have this criticism to make of the manner in which the committee proceeded. It put the cart before the horse. It heard a review from C.B.C. at the outset of its past administration. Then, without calling upon C.B.C. to outline its policy for the future, involving, as we eventually learned, the absorption of two major wave leangths now held by private companies in this country, it called upon the private companies to come forward and meet a case that had not yet been put before the two major wave lengths now held by private companies had been called upon to make their defence that C.B.C. was called upon to present its case. I say that was putting the cart before the horse. It put the private stations at a great disadvantage in not knowing adequately the case that they would be called upon later to meet. It also meant that we had

some major recommendations from C.B.C., which have found their way into the report and into the bill, but which did not come before the committee until the very last minute. For that I do not put any blame whatever on the corporation, because I am satisfied that its officials would have liked to make their complete presentation at the beginning and proceed in an orderly fashion. I place the blame entirely on the majority of the committee.
There is in the report one recommendation which is unanimous, and that is that a radio committee should be appointed every year and meet early in the session. Since parliamentary committees began to study radio in 1932, radio committees have met in nine out of the fifteen years. When years passed without a committee, when the committee eventually did sit it found it had a great deal of work to cover.
The second part of that recommendation will, I hope, be given due weight. The committee which sat this year did not meet until the seventy-fifth day of the session. This has meant that much of th,e work of the committee was done in these recent days under pressure and that a bill which raises issues of vast importance to the people of Canada now comes before the house at the very end of the session when there is a disposition to hurry through to prorogation.
It has been the practice in recent years for reports from the radio committee not to be the subject of discussion in the house. The first two committees of 1932 and 1934 submitted their reports to the house and a motion for concurrence in them was made in each case, and adopted. That, I submit, is the proper practice. In 1936 the committee's report was not concurred in by motion, but was followed by the enactment of the present Canadian Broadcasting Act of that year. The committee reports of 1938, 1939, 1942 and 1943 were not followed by any discussion in the house. I think that was a mistake. The report of 1944 was followed by one slight amendment to the act. I wish to express my conviction that the whole question of radio broadcasting is of such importance that it ought to receive adequate debate in this house. It would be good for the public and parliament to have more light and more information by way of an accounting on the part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and of the private stations of their operations. I think it can be said for C.B.C. that it would be glad to have more assistance from parliament. It has not had that assistance from parliament. There have been certain recom-

Radio Broadcasting
mendations from parliamentary committees, but the. committees' reports have not for the last ten years been given the concurrence of the house. The committees' recommendations have not been endorsed by the house, let alone by parliament. I think that C.B.C. is entitled to have from parliament some clear direction as to policy.
This point I make in favour of the bill. It affords us at long last an opportunity to review C.B.C. policy, particularly in relation to the major expansion that is now proposed.
In saying what I have to say, I wish to make it clear that when I speak critically I am not speaking critically of any individuals. I am speaking of the system which is implicit in the statute and of the policy which has been followed in the light of reports of committees. So far as I personally am concerned, in the course of the meetings of the committee I formed a liking and no little esteem for the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation who appeared before us, and I want to make it clear that any criticism I have to make is a criticism of a system and not of individuals.
There have been reports-and perhaps when the minister speaks he will say a word about this-about lobbying which sought to exert pressure on the committee. I found such a suggestion contained, for instance, in a letter dated August 2, 1946, written by the secretary of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture to certain groups. It contains this paragraph, and there were many other letters of the same kind sent throughout the country, some of which came to the attention of the committee. The paragraph reads:
Never before lias there been so strong a lobby on behalf of the private radio interests. A great deal of money has been made by these interests, despite anything that may be said to the contrary, and they are not hesitant about laying out money. The lobbying that has been going on is terrific, with suites at the chateau and a good deal of entertainment. We have been told that those private interests concerned, who are supporters of the government, are making it uncomfortable for the government and leaders of the parties. This is the old game of pressure politics with selfish interests attempting to again wield their influence.
I do not know where the writer of that letter got his information, but I want to say for myself as a member of the committee that I attended twenty-six out of the twenty-eight meetings and I saw not one trace at any time of any lobbying in any way, shape or form. I hope that the minister when he speaks will be able to say the same thing on behalf of those who sit on that side of the house. I think that when the radio committee is set up next year an effort should be made to
find the source of such utterly unfounded statements, because they are an unwarranted reflection on members of parliament who are seeking to do their best without paying any attention to any pressure. At no time did I see any sign of any pressure or any lobbying.
I have said that this bill calls upon us to see in perspective the policy that C.B.C. is following at the present time. I will review the history of recent years as rapidly as I can.
Parliament's concern with radio broadcasting really begins with the year 1929, when the Aird commission made its report to the then minister of marine, Hon. P. J. A. Cardin. That commission was composed of Sir John Aird, Mr. Charles A. Bowman, and Doctor Augustin Frigon, who is now general manager of the corporation. They recommended that a national company be formed, to be called the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Company, to own and operate all radio broadcasting stations in Canada. In other words, they recommended the complete nationalization of all means of broadcasting in Canada; they condemned direct advertising on the air, and recommended provincial control over programmes of stations within the provincial areas. No action was taken on that report until the year 1932, when a parliamentary committee was set up to review the whole situation. That committee made extensive recommendations which found their way into the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act of that year. There are in that report two leading recommendations which I think are deserving of mention at this time:
(b)	That -a nationally-owned system of radio broadcasting be instituted,-
I emphasize that.
-and that all stations required for its proper organization be eventually acquired, same to be financed from the revenue accruing to the business of broadcasting, without expense to the taxpayers through the public treasury.
(c)	That all stations, 100 watt and under, not required for the national system, remain under private ownership, but be regulated as to programmes and advertising by the rules of the commission.
Whereas the Aird commission had recommended seven powerful stations of 50,000 watts each, one to be located in the mari-times, one in each of the other provinces, the 1932 committee recommended five 50,000 watt stations and a number of privately owned 100 watt stations.
When the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act was enacted in 1932 certain safeguards were reserved to parliament which I think are of high importance. Section 9 of that act states that the commission shall have
Radio Broadcasting

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
power to carry on the business of broadcasting in Canada, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may:
(b)	acquire existing private stations either by lease, or, subject to the approval of parliament, by purchase;
(c)	subject to the approval of parliament, construct such new stations as may be required;
(g) subject to the approval of parliament, take over all broadcasting in Canada.
I emphasize those words, "subject to the approval of parliament," in reference to each of these powers.
Then we come to the 1934 committee, which included 'as recommendation No. 5 of its report:
That, pending the nationalization of all stations, greater cooperation should be established between privately owned stations and the commission.
Hon. members will see that still the underlying conception there is complete nationalization of all means of radio broadcasting in Canada.
The 1936 committee in its report included as its recommendation No. 7:
We reaffirm the principle of complete nationalization of radio broadcasting in Canada.
I point out that the report of 1936 was followed by the enactment of the present act. the Canadian Broadcasting Act of 1936, under which the Canadian Broadcasting corporation derives all its powers and functions to-day and that act was based on the recommendation of a committee which still contemplated the complete nationalization of all means of radio broadcasting in Canada.
Then we come to the 1938 report, and we find on page 194 this statement:
Your committee is of the opinion that while private stations will continue to serve a useful local purpose, the corporation urgently requires its own comprehensive facilities for distribution.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to give attention to the fact that here, in the 1938 report, some status is now accorded to the private stations, and here we have what I submit is the first departure in committee reports from the idea of complete nationalization; here we have the first recognition in a parliamentary report of a permanent role for private stations.
When we come to the next report, in the year 1939, we see emphasis is laid in the recommendations on the duty of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to coordinate both types of broadcasting; that is to say, national broadcasting over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and broadcasting over the private stations. It assumes that there is to be broadcasting from private stations to be coordinated

with the national system. The only inference is that a permanent role is now contemplated for the private stations.
Then we come to the 1942 report, which is a major report, which reaffirmed many of the recommendations of earlier committees as follows:
(a) The paramount importance of a single national authority to control all broadcasting in the public interest; (1932)
(ib) The public ownership of all high power stations under a national system of broadcasting, with low power stations _ individually operated or coordinated in relation to the dominant system; (1932)
(c) The coordination of all broadcasting in Canada through exclusive control being vested in the natiopally-owned system of:-
(i)	The character of all programmes, political or otherwise, broadcast by all stations and of the advertising content thereof; and
(ii)	All wire-line networks used for carrying broadcast programmes. (1936)
The report of the committee in 1943 reaffirmed those recommendations. The reports of the committees in both those years, 1942 and 1943, had this to say, that they recognized that private stations were serving a useful function. No longer do we find any suggestion of complete nationalization of all stations and all means of broadcasting in Canada.
In the report of the committee for 1943 we have for the first time set out a submission of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. It is done, it is true, without comment; but again there is the recognition that the private stations serve a useful function.
In the 1944 report the submission of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, representing the great majority of the private stations, asking for "an impartial" body to regulate broadcasting, was set forth, and this time it was rejected.
In the 1946 committee's report we have this statement:
Your committee feels that it would be less than fair if it did not record its view that private stations are giving good community service.
Also':
We are of the opinion that private stations should be at all times encouraged and aided to improve their service to their respective communities.
Having reviewed that history from 1929 to 1946, important years and years of great development in broadcasting in Canada, I say that we have six principles on which, I think, all parties in this house will agree.
The first is that radio broadcasting, being carried over the public domain, must be publicly controlled. The second is that in the adminstration of public control the public interest is to be the supreme consideration. In

Radio Broadcasting
the third place, broadcasting is to be Canadian. The public system was designed, among other reasons, for the purpose of ensuring that there would be carried over a national network in Canada programmes which would be Canadian in their content, and that any national system would not be dominated by * broadcasting from the United States. In the fourth place, broadcasting was to be designed to assist the development of Canadian talent. In the fifth place, the radio was to be recognized as an agency of education, not merely one of entertainment. In the sixth place, advertising was not to be permitted to mar programmes.
I say that these are principles on which, I think, all parties in this house will agree. I say also that there has been over these years an evolution and development in radio which has been characterized by these features. In the first place, there have been great technical advances, and advances also in the business of radio broadcasting. In the second place, it is recognized that we are now on the threshold of further great technical advances in radio. Frequency modulation and other discoveries open great vistas for the development of radio in Canada. In the third place, it is abundantly clear, and it is recognized, I submit, in these parliamentary reports to which I have referred, that the private stations have made a great contribution to radio broadcasting in Canada. They have established their right to a permanent role in our scheme of broadcasting in Canada; they have established their right to participate in the technical advances which lie before us; and thejr have established their value as competition for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; and as they develop they are entitled to fair play in that competitive role.
There were, according to the evidence submitted to the committee, to be found at page 165 of the proceedings, on June 6 of this year 103 private stations in Canada, having a strength ranging from 50 to 15,000 watts. Now, Mr. Speaker, obviously credit in measure is due to the enterprise of these stations themselves, which must have given public service to expand that way, and credit is also due for the opportunity given to them to develop under the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and also, I think, to the Department of Transport. I think it is clear that there has been an evolution in policy in the direction of permitting freer opportunity for the development of private stations. That has been all to the good, because I emphasize again that the 1936 act was written on the basis of the recommendations of a committee of parliament which affirmed the principle of
complete nationalization, and to that extent we have moved some distance away from the principle of the 1936 act.
I come now to a different subject, one that has to do with the position of private companies in relation to their wave lengths or frequencies. Both the 1943 and the 1946 reports urged that private stations be encouraged to improve their service to the public. How will they do this? Under present legislation what tenure is offered to them of their frequencies? They enjoy an annual licence. Under the Radio Act of 1938 power is given the minister to determine the duration and character of the licence. Regulation 5 issued under that act provides that the licence shall in each case terminate on March 31 of each year; if you will read section 11, subsection 5 of the Broadcasting Act, you will see that there is no vested interest on the part of the licensee in his frequency, and in the event of the frequency being taken over by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, either by expropriation or otherwise, he has no right to compensation.
Two views can be taken of the tenure of wave length or frequency by private stations. The first is that if the licensee has given good public service he is entitled to a renewal of his licence; the other view is that he has no right whatever, and his licence, and the development of his service to the public under the licence, must be circumscribed by that doomsday which he faces all the time, the 31st day of March of the following year. When we are calling upon private stations to improve their service, I ask, what encouragement is given them if they are to have nothing but insecurity of tenure? If their claim to frequency hangs by such a thread that it may be taken away from them on the next March 31; if there is no assurance that in the event of their giving good service and behaving themselves and adhering to the regulations their licence will be extended, what hope is there for the development of good broadcasting over private stations? There is this sword of Damocles hanging over the head of everyone of these stations, under such circumstances, and if the 1946 committee means what it says in asking that encouragement be given by parliament, or by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to the development of broadcasting over private stations, then a study must be made, without delay, of the question of tenure of wave length, subject to proper safeguards in the public interest, with respect to private stations. It is useless to expect them to develop their stations and expend large amounts of money on improve-
Radio Broadcasting

speechtext:
ments and giving better public service, as we wish them to do, if their tenure is to be so insecure.
My next point is that whatever confidence the private stations might have had in their tenure of frequency, subject to good behaviour, that confidence must have been greatly shaken by the series of actions of the corporation with reference to three wave lengths, 860, held by CFRB, (Toronto); 1010, CFCN, (Calgary) and 990, CKY, (Winnipeg).
I wish to refer to the North-American Regional broadcasting agreement signed at Havana in 1937, commonly known as the Havana agreement. It came into effect on January 30, 1941 and assigned to Canada six wave lengths known as Class 1-A channels. They are 690, which under the agreement is to be located in the province of Quebec, 740 in Ontario, 860 in Ontario, 990 in Manitoba, 1010 in Alberta and 1580 in Quebec. These frequencies, under the agreement, are to be developed to a strength of 50,000 watts. At the present time, and in fact during all these years, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has occupied three of these channels, being the three not held by the three private stations I have mentioned. It has developed its three 1-A frequencies to a strength of 50,000 watts, while the one held by CKY was 15,000 watts, and CFCN and CFRB, 10,000 watts eaoh. The Havana agreement has been extended by an agreement entered into in Washington on February 25 of this year, so that Canada has until the meeting of the international conference in this country in September, 1947, to develop all these six channels to a strength of 50,000 watts.
One point that should be understood by every member is that there is no requirement under the Havana treaty that these lengths should be held by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The corporation now proposes to take over these three wave lengths held by the three stations I have mentioned, and in so doing it is carrying out a matter of its own policy because it is not required to do so by the treaty. When the treaty came into effect in 1941 the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was not in a position to take over these three wave lengths.

subtopic: CORPORATION TO RECEIVE LICENCE FEES- ADVANCES ON ACCOUNT OF CAPITAL EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was dealing with the intention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to take 
over the wave lengths now possessed by stations CFRB in Toronto, CFCN in Calgary and CKY in Winnipeg, the first two of which have a power of 10,000 watts and the third of which has a power of 15,000 watts. CKY is actually owned by the government of Manitoba, which has not entered any objection to the assumption of its wave length by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, so that the matter at issue narrows down to whether the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation shall take over the wave lengths now possessed by stations CFRB and CFCN.
Before the six o'clock recess, I had mentioned that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation now takes the position that in 1941, when the Havana treaty came into effect, it was not in a position to occupy these three channels and, therefore, assigned them to these stations. This was done, first by a wire dated February 4, 1941, and then by a confirming letter, dated February 10, 1941, which will be found at pages 648 and 649 of the evidence before the 1946 committee. There is not one word in either the wire or the confirming letter, or in any subsequent correspondence with these stations to the end of 1945, suggesting that these channels were being assigned only for a temporary purpose, or for the duration of the war, or until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation could obtain equipment and proceed with its expansion. There is no suggestion of that; the communications simply announce the assignment of these wave lengths to these companies. In the autumn of 1945 the licensees in question were told that the matter was under review, and were invited to attend a meeting of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at which this matter was discussed. The first official notification to them was by letter dated April 18, 1946, that next spring their channels are to be taken over by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
There is a conflict of evidence as between the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the one hand and the officials of these stations on the other, as to certain facts in regard to the notice, if any, implied or otherwise, which these companies are said to have had as to the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in reference to the assumption of these class 1-A channels. On the one hand, these licensees say they had no knowledge of any policy under which it was the intention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to take their channels. They say they thought they were secure in those channels, subject to giving good public service; that they developed their wave lengths on that basis, expended money to develop them,

Radio Broadcasting
and that if they were to be dispossessed it would have been far better for them if they ' had not been assigned these channels in 1941, because the spectrum is so full now-more than it was in 1941-that they would have had a better choice of alternative channels in 1941 than it is possible for them to have today. Moreover, the alternative wave lengths now offered to them by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are admittedly not as good as those they now enjoy. In the case of CFRB it is proposed that they go to the end of the dial, at 1550, which is described among technical radio people as "the graveyard" of the dial. Then, in the case of CFRB it means an expenditure of some $300,000 for simply moving their broadcasting facilities to the point where they must move now, near Niagara, away from Aurora, outside Toronto, where they are now, according to the statement made to the committee by the general manager of CFRB. It means, also, that CBC, which has been a competitor of CFRB in the great metropolitan area of central Ontario, will move into the space where its competitor formerly did business. It means it will have open to it all the listener contacts and a first-class opportunity to obtain the commercial contacts and Columbia network heretofore enjoyed by CFRB. It means also for both CFRB and CFCN a smaller listener-coverage under the proposed new wave lengths.
It is admitted on all sides that these stations have a good record of public service in all respects. I am not going to take time to enumerate their record; it was demonstrated that these stations had an enviable record of public service. As to ownership, in the case of CFCN there is a proposal for a wide diffusion of ownership among farm organizations in the province of Alberta. CFRB is owned by the Rogers Radio Broadcasting Company, and not more than ten per cent of the stock of that company is in the hands of any one person; it is widely diffused. Both these licensees were pioneers in radio; both took very hard knocks in the days when it was difficult for radio broadcasting companies to survive; and having survived and built up their stations, they are to have their wave lengths taken away from them.
I want to be fair to all parties. On the other hand, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation say it was always their policy to take over all these class 1-A channels under the Havana treaty. They say the policy was always known and the execution or fufilment of the policy was simply delayed because, owing to war conditions, they could not obtain equipment to proceed with their plans. They refer to an endorsement put on the licences 63260-333
of these three licensees, beginning in 1941. I pause there to say that the endorsement did nothing more than call attention to one of the regulations under the act, which simply provides, as I intimated earlier, that the assignment of a channel is effective only until March 31 of the following year. That endorsement did not tell these licensees that it was the policy of CJ3.C. to assume their channels. The reference to the regulation was a reference to a regulation which is the law for every station in the Dominion of Canada. It was not peculiar in any respect to these three stations. I was surprised to hear an official of the Department of Transport rely on that, as an alleged notice to these licensees, that it was the policy of the CJ3.C. to take their frequencies when it suited the CJ3.C. to do so. The endorsement was suggested by the Controller of Radio in the Department of Transport in a letter dated April 30, 1941. It was approved on behalf of the C.B.C. in a letter which we were told in evidence was not approved by the board of the C.B.C., but was simply written by the executive assistant to the then general manager. There was very clear understanding between the Department of Transport on the one hand and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the other. The correspondence shows clearly that they understood at the time that it was settled policy to take those channels when it suited the C.B.C. to do so. They took the utmost care to make it a matter of record in the correspondence exchanged beween the Department of Transport and the C.B.C. That is as plain as the nose on one's face; but for some reason or another, it did not occur to anybody to put so much as a phrase in a letter addressed to these three licensees to indicate that this was the policy of the department.
